title: Biologic Side Effects: Infection, Reactions and Monitoring
meta_title: Biologic Side Effects: Infection and Safety Monitoring
meta_description: Biologic safety: urgent infection and allergy symptoms, injection and infusion reactions, and what to agree about monitoring and your next dose.
excerpt: Know when to get urgent help, why biologic precautions differ, and what to agree with your rheumatology team about infections and monitoring.
direct_answer: Biologic medicines can increase infection risk and cause injection-site or infusion reactions. Some symptoms need emergency help, while others need prompt advice before your next dose. Know your exact medicine, keep its alert card, and agree a written monitoring and infection plan. Do not use a general article to decide when to stop or restart treatment.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: biologic side effects, biologic infection risk, injection infusion reaction, biologic monitoring, rheumatoid arthritis medicines
content:
Biologic medicines can control inflammatory arthritis, but their effects on the immune system mean that infections and other side effects need a clear plan. A small injection-site reaction is different from a serious allergy, and a new hot joint is not automatically an arthritis flare. Know the name of your medicine, keep its alert card, and use the urgent routes below rather than waiting for your next routine appointment.

Urgent symptoms: act now

Call 999 for a possible serious allergic reaction: sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; or collapse. Use your prescribed adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, following its instructions, and call 999. A rash is not required. Do not take another dose after a suspected serious allergy unless the treating team has assessed you and told you it is safe. See NHS anaphylaxis advice.

Call 999 for possible sepsis or stroke: infection with confusion, slurred speech, very fast or difficult breathing, or blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin needs emergency help. Sudden face droop, arm weakness or speech difficulty also means 999, even if it improves. Do not wait to find out whether the medicine caused it. See NHS sepsis and stroke symptoms.

A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent assessment, even without fever. Difficulty moving it or bearing weight can be a sign of joint infection, not just a flare. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 in England, Scotland or Wales. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. If you also have emergency symptoms, call 999. NHS septic arthritis advice explains why early treatment matters.

Who this article is for

This guide is for adults taking a biologic for inflammatory arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Examples include adalimumab and other TNF inhibitors, rituximab and tocilizumab. It is not a complete list of medicines or side effects, and their precautions are not interchangeable. JAK inhibitors are targeted synthetic DMARDs, not biologics; read our separate JAK inhibitor guide if that is your treatment.

Use the leaflet for your exact brand, device and formulation, together with your team's instructions. The same medicine may also treat other conditions at different doses. A side-effect list is not a prediction of what will happen to you, and this page cannot compare your personal risks against the benefits of controlling arthritis.

Infection: get advice before the next dose

Report possible infection promptly to your rheumatology team or GP: a new persistent cough, hot painful or spreading skin redness, painful urination, an infected wound, dental infection, fever, chills or feeling unusually unwell. Redness can be harder to see on darker skin, so warmth, tenderness, swelling and how you feel also matter. If you cannot reach the team and need urgent advice, use the urgent-care routes above. Do not wait for a routine blood test or for a fever to appear.

Tocilizumab can lessen signs of inflammation and suppress C-reactive protein (CRP). A reassuring CRP result does not by itself rule out infection during treatment. Tell anyone assessing you that you take it. This warning comes from its UK product information; it is a medicine-specific point, not a reason to dismiss symptoms on any other biologic.

There is no universal cold, antibiotic or restart rule for every biologic. Serious active infection can require treatment interruption, but the decision depends on the medicine and illness. Contact the prescribing team before a dose or infusion when you have an infection, are taking antibiotics, or have been told to pause. Follow the written sick-day plan or exact product leaflet while obtaining advice. Do not decide from this article to inject as normal, stop indefinitely, restart after a fixed number of days or double a later dose. If you have no plan and a dose is due, seek same-day advice rather than guessing. The MabThera leaflet, for example, asks RA patients to report even a mild infection before an infusion.

Tell your team promptly about a cough that does not go away, unexplained weight loss or night sweats. Screening before treatment reduces some risks but does not make tuberculosis impossible later. Report a known infection exposure too, so the team can decide whether you need assessment or preventive treatment. A Humira patient leaflet describes tuberculosis and hepatitis B precautions; these are not tests to arrange or interpret on your own.

Injection-site and infusion reactions are different

With injected adalimumab, itching, redness and pain around the injection site are recognised common side effects. A small local reaction does not automatically mean a dangerous allergy. Ask your nurse or pharmacist if it bothers you, persists or keeps recurring. Get prompt assessment for a reaction that is worsening, very painful, hot or spreading, especially if you feel unwell: infection and allergy cannot be reliably distinguished from a description alone. Emergency allergy symptoms need 999.

Use the sites and technique you were taught, rotate sites, and follow the exact leaflet for storage and any time out of the fridge. Do not use heat, hot water or a microwave to warm a syringe or pen. Different products have different instructions, so do not copy another brand's waiting time or injection method. The NHS adalimumab information and your own leaflet can help you prepare questions for your nurse.

During an infusion, tell the nurse immediately about any new symptom, including flushing, itching, chills, rash, chest tightness, breathlessness or dizziness. Staff decide whether to slow or stop the infusion and what treatment is needed. Do not wait until it finishes. Rituximab reactions can also occur within 24 hours of an infusion; follow your unit's aftercare plan, and use 999 for serious allergy symptoms after leaving.

Important risks depend on the medicine

  • Adalimumab, a TNF inhibitor: the leaflet highlights tuberculosis and hepatitis B reactivation, worsening heart failure and problems affecting the protective covering of nerves. New or worsening breathlessness, swollen feet, vision changes, weakness or numbness need prompt medical advice. Sudden stroke symptoms or severe breathing difficulty need 999. New or changing skin lesions should also be checked. Its cancer warnings do not mean that every lump is cancer, or that every biologic carries an identical risk.
  • Rituximab: infection, hepatitis B reactivation and infusion reactions are important. Very rarely, a serious brain infection called progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) can occur. New problems with memory, thinking, walking or vision need immediate medical advice, not the next clinic visit. Sudden one-sided weakness or speech problems still follow the 999 stroke route. See the patient leaflet and alert card.
  • Tocilizumab: blood-cell, liver and cholesterol changes need monitoring. New severe abdominal pain, or abdominal pain with unexplained bowel changes or fever, needs urgent medical assessment because intestinal complications can occur. Do not wait for every symptom to appear. Its patient leaflet also explains allergy and infection warnings.

These examples are not a checklist that makes other medicines risk-free. Take persistent or worrying new symptoms to a clinician, and bring the full medicine list, including methotrexate, steroids, non-prescription medicines and supplements. Do not apply a warning or monitoring schedule from one biologic to another.

Monitoring and prevention: agree your own plan

Before treatment, screening can include tuberculosis and hepatitis checks according to the drug and your history. During treatment, blood tests and reviews depend on the biologic, other medicines and your results. For example, tocilizumab requires checks of liver enzymes, blood cells and lipids. Ask which tests you need, who orders them, who reads the results and what happens if a test is missed or abnormal. Feeling well does not replace monitoring; normal monitoring does not replace assessment of new symptoms.

Discuss vaccines before starting treatment and before future appointments. Non-live vaccines can be used during immunosuppressive treatment, although protection can be reduced. Live vaccines usually need specialist advice and are generally avoided during biologic treatment. Timing matters particularly with rituximab because it affects antibody-producing B cells. Agree the timing with the team rather than moving infusions or stopping medicines yourself. NRAS explains rituximab and vaccination. Ask your GP or vaccination service about the current NHS programme for your age, medicines and UK nation; older online eligibility tables may be out of date.

Tell your team before surgery, invasive dental treatment, pregnancy or trying for a baby. There is no single stopping rule for all biologics. Pregnancy exposure may also affect the timing of a baby's live vaccines, so tell the maternity and infant vaccination teams which drug you used and when.

A useful one-page safety plan

Keep the drug's generic and brand names, the last and next dose dates, your alert card, the rheumatology advice number and its opening hours. Ask for a written answer to: what to do with an infection before the next dose; who to contact out of hours; which symptoms need immediate assessment; and who authorises restarting after a pause. Keep your monitoring dates and a current medicine list with it.

You can report a suspected side effect through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme; you do not need to be certain the medicine caused it. Reporting does not replace medical care or emergency help. This article is general UK information, not an individual treatment or restart plan.

key_takeaways: Call 999 for serious allergy, possible sepsis or stroke symptoms. A hot swollen joint needs urgent assessment even without fever.
Precautions differ by medicine. Tocilizumab can suppress CRP; normal results do not by themselves rule out infection.
Agree infection, monitoring and restart instructions with your team. There is no universal cold or antibiotic rule for every biologic.
